notes.front: What is the December 2020 edition of the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The edition before the current May 2025 one; it is now a historical version, but older study materials still quote it.
notes.explanation: Wording from 2020 that the 2025 edition changed can mislead you if you learn from an older source.
notes.example: The Kanban Pocket Guide (2022) quotes the 2020 wording, such as Work Item Age ending at the “current time”.
notes.source: Kanban Guides, “History” of The Kanban Guide
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated on the page; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the “2025 Adaptations” section of the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The Guide's own list, on its last page, of what changed in the May 2025 edition.
notes.explanation: It is the authoritative summary of how the current Guide differs from the December 2020 edition.
notes.example: One entry reads that Kanban Measures were renamed Flow Metrics.

notes.front: What is the Open Guide to Kanban?
notes.back: An expanded adaptation of the May 2025 Kanban Guide by John Coleman (July 2025 edition), with its own edition history.
notes.explanation: Kanban Guides publishes it alongside the Kanban Guide, which remains the minimal reference.
notes.example: Kanban Guides describes it as a community-expanded handbook, and the Kanban Guide as the minimal, official reference.
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated on the page; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: To which production system does the Kanban Guide trace the present state of Kanban?
notes.back: The Toyota Production System (and its antecedents).
notes.explanation: The Guide also names Taiichi Ohno and W. Edwards Deming in this history.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “History of Kanban”, p. 8

notes.front: Which two people does the Kanban Guide name in Kanban's history?
notes.back: Taiichi Ohno and W. Edwards Deming.
notes.explanation: The Guide traces Kanban to the Toyota Production System and their work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “History of Kanban”, p. 8

notes.front: Where and when does the Guide say the practices for knowledge work now called Kanban mostly originated?
notes.back: On a team at Corbis, in 2006.
notes.explanation: The practices then spread to a large international community that kept evolving them.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “History of Kanban”, p. 8

notes.front: What are the editions of The Kanban Guide, oldest first?
notes.back: July 2020, December 2020 and May 2025.
notes.explanation: Kanban Guides lists the May 2025 edition as the current, living document and the two 2020 editions as historical versions.
notes.source: Kanban Guides, “History” of The Kanban Guide
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated on the page; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What is the current edition of The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The May 2025 edition, dated 1 May 2025.
notes.explanation: Kanban Guides calls it a living document, updated 1 May 2025; always check the date of any Guide you study from.
notes.source: Kanban Guides, “History” of The Kanban Guide
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated on the page; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the Kanban Guide's Endnote say must be preserved?
notes.back: The minimum set of practices and metrics, and the spirit of optimizing value.
notes.explanation: Everything else can be added to or adapted around this minimum.

notes.front: May a team add other principles, methodologies and techniques to its Kanban system?
notes.back: Yes. The Endnote says one can, and likely should, as long as the minimum is preserved.
notes.explanation: Kanban is meant to be a minimal core that other approaches can build on.

notes.front: What did the 2025 edition add to convey the intent of terms such as stakeholder, value and risk?
notes.back: Conventions for Kanban, Kanban system, stakeholder, value, risk, visualize and visualization.
notes.explanation: The conventions say how these terms are meant in the Guide, without replacing other definitions.

notes.front: In the 2025 edition, for whom can value realization be?
notes.back: Stakeholders, including but not limited to customers.
notes.explanation: In 2020 an effective workflow delivered what “customers” want; in 2025 it delivers what “stakeholders” want.

notes.front: How did the 2025 edition change the definition of Kanban?
notes.back: It made it simpler, specifically as it pertains to knowledge work, dropping “that uses a visual, pull-based system”.
notes.explanation: The 2020 definition ended “…through a process that uses a visual, pull-based system”.

notes.front: Where did the SLE move to in the 2025 edition?
notes.back: Into the Definition of Workflow section.
notes.explanation: In December 2020 the SLE had its own subsection under actively managing items.

notes.front: How did the 2025 edition change the wording on how WIP is controlled?
notes.back: It became less explicit, and hence more flexible.
notes.explanation: The 2020 edition said control was usually shown as numbers or slots called WIP limits; 2025 allows any representation.

notes.front: Which three topics did the 2025 edition become more explicit about?
notes.back: Multiple DoWs, variation, and connecting flow to value realization.
notes.explanation: For example, the 2025 Guide encourages a DoW wherever members need to connect flow to value realization.

notes.front: What did the 2025 edition do to the three practices, and which word does it use more often?
notes.back: It simplified the three practices and mentions “select” (items) more often.
notes.explanation: Selecting items when there is capacity is how the pull system is described.

notes.front: In 2025 the section called Kanban Measures was renamed {{c1::Flow Metrics}}.
notes.explanation: The four mandatory metrics themselves are the same: WIP, Throughput, Work Item Age and Cycle Time.

notes.front: What did the 2025 edition make more explicit about flow metric names?
notes.back: The flexibility to call the metrics by other names.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Guide gives examples: Cycle Time could be Flow Time, Throughput could be Delivery Rate.

notes.front: What reference did the 2025 edition delete from the Guide?
notes.back: The reference to Kanban being immutable.
notes.explanation: The 2020 Endnote said Kanban's practices and measures were immutable, and that implementing only parts of Kanban is not Kanban.

notes.front: Which form of active management listed in the December 2020 edition is gone from the 2025 edition?
notes.back: Avoiding work items piling up in any part of the workflow.
notes.explanation: The 2020 edition listed four forms; the 2025 edition lists three.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (December 2020), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: How did the 2025 edition change where Work Item Age ends?
notes.back: From “the current time” (2020) to “the current date” (2025).
notes.explanation: Materials that quote the 2020 wording, such as the Pocket Guide, still say “current time”.

notes.front: A study note says: “Kanban's practices are immutable; implementing only parts of Kanban is not Kanban.” Is that the current Guide?
notes.back: No. That is December 2020 wording; the 2025 edition deleted the reference to immutability.
notes.choices:
A) Yes, it is the May 2025 Endnote
B) No, it is December 2020 wording
C) No, it comes from the Kanban Method
notes.choicesExplained: A: the 2025 Endnote says other principles, methodologies and techniques can be added but the minimum must be preserved. It does not call Kanban immutable. C: it is the Kanban Guide's own 2020 Endnote.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Adaptations list says the reference to immutability was deleted.

notes.front: A training slide lists four forms of active management, including “avoid items piling up”. Which edition is it based on?
notes.back: The December 2020 edition; the 2025 edition lists three forms.
notes.explanation: Always check which edition a source quotes; the current edition is May 2025.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (December 2020), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A practice question quotes the Guide's definition as “a strategy… that uses a visual, pull-based system”. Which edition is that?
notes.back: The December 2020 edition; the 2025 definition stops at “the flow of value through a process”.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Adaptations list a simpler definition, specifically as it pertains to knowledge work.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (December 2020), “Definition of Kanban”, p. 4

notes.front: A colleague says the current Guide says WIP control is usually shown as WIP limits. Is that right?
notes.back: No. That was 2020 wording; the 2025 edition lets control be represented in any way the members deem appropriate.
notes.explanation: The 2025 Adaptations made how WIP is controlled less explicit and more flexible.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Actively Managing Items in a Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: A team keeps its board and flow metrics but stops controlling WIP. Does it still meet the Guide's Endnote?
notes.back: No. The minimum set of practices and metrics must be preserved, and controlling WIP is part of that minimum.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires members to control WIP explicitly; adding things is fine, removing the minimum is not.

notes.front: Are “Start with what you do now” and classes of service part of the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: No. They come from Kanban University's Kanban Method, a different body of knowledge.
notes.explanation: The Kanban Guide has three practices and four flow metrics; it mentions neither change-management principles nor classes of service. Classes of service are different handling rules for different kinds of work, such as an urgent lane that jumps the queue (Kanban Method).
notes.contrast: The Kanban Method adds principles, six general practices, lead time and classes of service.

notes.front: Is the Open Guide to Kanban the same as the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: No. It is an expanded adaptation of the May 2025 Kanban Guide, with its own authorship and edition history.
notes.explanation: Kanban Guides presents the Kanban Guide as the minimal reference and the Open Guide as expanded guidance.
notes.sourceLicence: C · no licence stated on the page; facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Is “Pull the oldest work first” a rule in the Kanban Guide?
notes.back: No. It is advice in ProKanban's web reader summary, not text from the Guide.
notes.explanation: ProKanban's reader adds its own summaries and glosses around the Guide; quote the PDF for the Guide's wording.
notes.contrast: The Guide requires controlling WIP and managing age, but sets no pull order.
